Wont
WUNT or WAHNT
adj. or n. (past participle of obsolete won, “to be accustomed”)
From Old English gewunod, past participle of gewunian (to be accustomed, dwell). The verb won in this sense is obsolete; wont survives as an adjective (he was wont to do thus) and a noun (as his wont was).

📖 Biblical Definition

Wont is the KJV’s archaic word for what is customarily or habitually done—a person’s settled practice, his usual pattern, the thing he was accustomed to do. The word survives in modern English chiefly in the phrase as is his wont; the KJV uses it across both testaments to render the Hebrew and Greek words for customary practice. Of the LORD Himself, of Christ, of the apostles, of various figures across Scripture, the verb captures the pattern: this was the manner from the beginning, as the manner of the priests was; and Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives (Luke 22:39); and he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read (Luke 4:16—custom there is the cousin word). The narrative function of wont is several. It captures the settled patterns of life that are the visible texture of any person’s discipleship—Christ’s wont of going to the Mount of Olives, His wont of synagogue attendance on the Sabbath, His wont of withdrawing to pray, His wont of teaching. It captures the institutional patterns by which the priestly orders or civic offices operated. It captures the personal patterns by which figures like Daniel were known—Daniel as he was wont opening his windows toward Jerusalem and praying three times a day, even when the decree forbade it. The narrative significance of wont is therefore important: it makes visible the long patterns of a life lived in a particular way, the disciplines that constitute the texture of discipleship, the personal and institutional habits that the LORD and His people maintain across the years. Where Scripture says of Christ as he was wont, it names a pattern that had become so settled in His earthly life that His disciples could predict where He would be in the evening, what He would do on the Sabbath, how He would withdraw to pray. The disciple’s life is to be similarly patterned: settled wonts of prayer, of Word, of gathering, of worship, of generosity, of confession, of family devotion—patterns the people who know him can name as what he is wont to do, and that constitute the long arc of faithful discipleship across his years.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WONT as accustomed; used; as in the phrase he was wont to do this; in scripture, used of Christ’s settled patterns of life (Mount of Olives, synagogue, prayer) and of the personal patterns of the saints.

expand to see more

WONT, a. or n. — Accustomed; used; as, he was wont to do this. And Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives (Luke 22:39).

WONT, v.i. — To be accustomed or habituated; to be used. (Now chiefly archaic; survives in the adjective and the phrase.)

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 22:39 — "And he came out, and went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed him."

Mark 10:1 — "And he arose from thence, and cometh into the coasts of Judaea by the farther side of Jordan: and the people resort unto him again; and, as he was wont, he taught them again."

Daniel 6:10 — "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."

Luke 4:16 — "And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Wont is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by its near-disappearance from modern English; the loss of the word coincides with the loss in the contemporary church of the rich category of settled patterns of life that the biblical wonts of Christ and the saints make visible.

expand to see more

Wont has nearly disappeared from modern English usage, surviving chiefly as a stylized phrase in literary writing. Modern translations replace it with custom, usually, habit, or rephrase the construction entirely. The vocabulary loss is small; the loss of the underlying category, however, is large. Wont names a settled pattern of life, the visible texture of disciplines maintained across years. Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives tells us not merely where He went that evening but what His pattern was—the long-settled habit of withdrawing to the Mount, predictable enough that His disciples followed without instruction and Judas knew where to find Him. The biblical narrative is rich with such wonts: Daniel’s windows-toward-Jerusalem prayer thrice daily; Christ’s synagogue attendance on every Sabbath; Paul’s reasoning in the synagogues on the Sabbath days; the patterns of life that constituted the visible discipleship of each.

The loss of the category in contemporary Christianity is a real pastoral concern. The believer often lives without settled wonts: prayer is fit in when convenient, Scripture-reading is sporadic, gathering is according to inclination, fasting is rare or non-existent, family worship is occasional rather than disciplined. The visible texture of discipleship—the patterns that the people who know him can name as what he is wont to do—has thinned to almost nothing. The recovery is the recovery of the disciplines themselves, settled over time into the patterns of life that Scripture describes of Christ and the saints. The KJV’s wont is therefore not merely a vocabulary item but a window into a discipleship category the contemporary church needs: the settled, predictable, long-pattern life that Christ Himself modeled and that the saints have always exhibited as the texture of mature faith. Recover the disciplines that make the word applicable, and the disciple recovers what it is to be wont to do the things that mark a life formed by Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English gewunod (accustomed), past participle of obsolete won (to be accustomed); preserved in the KJV in passages naming the settled patterns of life of Christ, Daniel, and the saints—the visible texture of discipleship.

expand to see more

Old English gewunian — to be accustomed, dwell; root of wont.

Greek ethō (G1486) — to be accustomed; used in Luke 4:16 (“as his custom was”).

Greek ethos (G1485) — custom, habit (Acts 17:2, Paul’s synagogue reasoning “as his manner was”).

Hebrew qūm + adverbial construction — conveying the habitual practice (often in narrative contexts of Daniel-type patterns).

Usage

"Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives—Christ’s settled pattern of evening withdrawal to the Mount, predictable enough that Judas knew where to find Him."

"Daniel’s windows-toward-Jerusalem prayer thrice daily and Christ’s Sabbath synagogue attendance are exemplars of biblical wonts: settled patterns of life as the visible texture of discipleship."

"Loss of the word and loss of the category coincide; recovery of disciplined patterns is recovery of what it means to be wont to do the things that mark a life formed by Christ."
